title: The finally block for cleanup operations

blocks.text: 3.1.3 The finally block for cleanup operations

The nightly settlement export fails at 02:10. The alert reads `java.io.IOException: flush failed: No space left on device`, thrown by the `finally` that closes the report writer. The real failure, a query that timed out, is in no log, and the next night's export blocks on an export lock that was never released.
finally Runs on Every Way Out of try: return, break, continue or a Throw
This loop leaves its `try` five ways, counting the normal end:

finally after .tmp
  finally after notes.txt
  finally after rates.csv
returned rates.csv
  finally after notes.txt
  finally after STOP
returned null
  finally after notes.txt
  finally after ""
threw empty name

The compiler copies the `finally` code onto every path out of the `try`: the normal end, each `return`, `break` and `continue`, and an exception of any type (`javap -c` shows five copies of the `println` in `firstCsv`).

Cleanup written anywhere else misses a path. A quote service counts calls in flight and refuses new ones at 200. If the decrement sits after the backend call, every failed call leaks one; add it to a `catch (IOException e)` as well, and every `NullPointerException` still leaks one. After an outage of a few minutes the gauge stays at 200 and the service refuses every request with nothing running. Unit 6.3.1 applies the same rule to `unlock()`.
A return in finally Throws Away the Exception and the try's Result

rowsImported(prices-0611.csv) = 0
version() = 2

The file was corrupt; the caller got 0 and no error, so its retry on `IOException` never ran. When `finally` ends with `return`, `break`, `continue` or a throw of its own, that ending replaces the `try`'s: the pending exception or return value is dropped. javac warns only when the `finally` lint is on (`-Xlint:finally` or `-Xlint`):
ReturnInFinally.java:16: warning: [finally] finally clause cannot complete normally
<!-- practice 1 -->
A return Fixes Its Value Before finally Runs, but the Object Can Still Change
A metrics buffer hands its lines to a collector every ten seconds and starts a new batch:

attemptsSoFar() = 3, attempts now 0
drain() = []

`return attempts` copied the value 3 before `finally` ran, so the reset didn't reach the caller. `return pending` copied a reference, and `clear()` emptied the list it points to, so every batch the collector got was empty. Reassigning the field leaves the returned list alone:
drainFixed() = [cpu=0.55, heap=0.47], pending now []
<!-- practice 2 -->
An Exception From finally Replaces the One in Flight and Skips the Cleanup After It
The export from the opening:

caller sees: java.io.IOException: flush failed: No space left on device
export lock still held: true

The `IOException` from `close()` replaced the `IllegalStateException`, which survives as neither cause nor suppressed. It also ended the `finally`, so `unlock()` never ran, and the next export, on another thread, waits for the lock forever.

flowchart TD
    L["exportLock.lock()"] --> W["out.write in try"]
    W --> Q["queryFailed() throws IllegalStateException"]
    Q --> F["finally starts"]
    F --> C["out.close() throws IOException"]
    C --> D["IllegalStateException dropped"]
    C --> S["exportLock.unlock() never runs"]
    C --> X["caller sees IOException"]
Each cleanup step that can fail needs its own `try`, and its failure is attached to the original with `addSuppressed`:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: settlement query timed out after 30 s
	at Replaced.queryFailed(Replaced.java:16)
	at Replaced.exportFixed(Replaced.java:35)
	at Replaced.main(Replaced.java:62)
	Suppressed: java.io.IOException: flush failed: No space left on device
		at Replaced$ReportWriter.close(Replaced.java:12)
		at Replaced.exportFixed(Replaced.java:41)
		... 1 more
export lock still held: false
When only `close()` fails, it is rethrown: a writer that couldn't flush lost rows, and swallowing that reports a file as complete when it isn't.
<!-- practice 3 -->
finally Runs Only When the Thread Leaves try: exit, halt and a Killed JVM Skip It
Each case runs in its own JVM: a shutdown hook prints `hook ran`, and a thread sleeps inside a `try` whose `finally` prints `finally ran`:

System.exit(0) in try:     exit   0  hook ran
halt(0) in try:            exit   0  (nothing)
main ends, daemon in try:  exit   0  hook ran
SIGTERM while in try:      exit 143  hook ran
SIGKILL while in try:      exit 137  (nothing)
interrupt() while in try:  exit   0  interrupted, finally ran, hook ran

`finally` runs when the thread leaves the `try`. `System.exit` and a SIGTERM start the JVM's shutdown: hooks run, then the JVM halts every thread where it is; per the `Runtime` javadoc, "`finally` clauses are not executed". When the last non-daemon thread ends, the same happens to daemon threads. `halt` and SIGKILL skip the hooks too. An interrupt is the one case here that runs `finally`: it ends the `sleep` with an exception, and the thread leaves `try` the ordinary way.

A lock file or temp file cleaned up only in `finally` is left behind by every deploy whose SIGTERM arrives while a thread is in that `try`. Cleanup that must survive shutdown goes in a shutdown hook that stops the work and waits for it (unit 6.4.1), and startup must cope with what a SIGKILL leaves.
<!-- practice 4 -->
Summary

items: **`finally` runs on every way out of `try`.** Cleanup after the block, or in a `catch`, misses the paths it wasn't written for.
**A `return` in `finally` discards the exception and the result.** javac warns only with `-Xlint:finally` or `-Xlint`.
**`return` fixes its value before `finally` runs.** Reassigning the variable doesn't change the result; mutating the object it refers to does.

**An exception from `finally` replaces the one in flight and ends the `finally`.** Give each failing cleanup step its own `try`, attach its failure with `addSuppressed`, and release locks in an inner `finally`.
**`finally` needs the thread to leave `try`.** `System.exit`, SIGTERM, `halt` and SIGKILL skip it, and so does JVM exit for a daemon thread still in `try`.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: A job holds a lock, a temp file and a database connection. Write its cleanup by hand so that each is released when any other release fails. How many nested `try` blocks did it take?
Your service gets SIGTERM, and a request is in the middle of a two-phase write. What should the shutdown hook wait for, and for how long?
Turn on `-Xlint:finally` in a codebase you know. What does it find?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Cleanup Is a Block of Code

C++ releases a resource in a destructor that runs when its owning object goes out of scope. Java objects have no such moment, so Java put cleanup in the method that acquires the resource, as a block the compiler copies onto every exit path. The release sits next to the acquisition, but each caller rewrites it, in order, with nested handling for each failing step. Try-with-resources (unit 3.1.4) moved that code into the compiler for anything `AutoCloseable`; `finally` stays for what is not a resource object: a lock, a gauge, a flag.
